Explain goroutines and channels - how do: A goroutine is a lightweight, Go-runtime-managed function execution - the Go scheduler multiplexes many goroutines (often thousands or more) onto a much smaller number of OS threads, with goroutines starting at only a few KB of stack (growable as needed) versus an OS thread's much larger fixed stack, making them dramatically cheaper to create and switch between. Channels are typed conduits for goroutines to communicate and synchronize safely by passing data, embodying Go's philosophy of 'share memory by communicating' rather than 'communicate by sharing memory' - reducing the need for explicit locks by using channels to hand off data ownership between goroutines instead.
What is the difference between a buffere: An unbuffered channel has no capacity - a send blocks until a receiver is ready to receive, and vice versa, providing strong synchronization guarantees (a successful send proves the receiver has received it). A buffered channel (`make(chan int, 10)`) can hold a fixed number of values without a receiver being immediately ready, only blocking sends once the buffer is full - useful for decoupling producer and consumer speeds somewhat, or for a known-bounded worker pool pattern, but it weakens the synchronization guarantee (a completed send only proves the value entered the buffer, not that anything has received it yet), which matters for correctness reasoning.
How does Go's `select` statement work wi: `select` waits on multiple channel operations simultaneously, proceeding with whichever case becomes ready first (if multiple are ready simultaneously, one is chosen pseudo-randomly to avoid starvation) - it's how Go implements handling several concurrent event sources (multiple channels, a timeout via `time.After`, a cancellation signal) without needing separate goroutines polling each one. A `default` case makes the select non-blocking, immediately proceeding if no channel is ready rather than waiting.
Explain Go's error handling philosophy (: Go treats errors as ordinary return values (typically the last return value, checked explicitly with `if err != nil`) rather than using exceptions that unwind the call stack. This makes error handling paths explicit and visible at every call site (you can see exactly where an error could occur and how it's handled by reading the code), at the cost of more verbose code with repeated `if err != nil` checks compared to try/catch-based languages. The tradeoff is intentional - Go's designers prioritized explicitness and predictable control flow over the more concise but less visible error propagation exceptions provide, believing forcing errors to be handled (or explicitly ignored) at each step produces more reliable code.
What is a Go interface, and how does Go': A Go interface defines a set of method signatures a type must implement; any type that has those methods automatically satisfies the interface, with no explicit `implements` declaration needed anywhere - this is structural typing (if it has the methods, it satisfies the interface) rather than Java/C#'s nominal typing, where a class must explicitly declare `implements InterfaceName`. This lets you define an interface after the fact and have existing types satisfy it retroactively without modifying them, enabling much more flexible, decoupled design where packages don't need to know about interfaces defined elsewhere in advance.
What is a race condition in Go, and how: A race condition occurs when multiple goroutines access shared memory concurrently, with at least one writing, without proper synchronization - leading to unpredictable, non-deterministic behavior that may work fine in testing and fail intermittently in production. Go's built-in race detector (`go test -race` or `go run -race`) instruments memory accesses at runtime and reports the exact goroutines and code locations involved in a detected race, making it dramatically easier to find than trying to reproduce and diagnose an intermittent concurrency bug manually - running tests with `-race` routinely (not just when a bug is suspected) is standard practice for any concurrent Go code.
Explain the difference between a pointer: A value receiver method operates on a copy of the struct, so any modification inside the method doesn't affect the original - use this for small, immutable-in-practice structs where copying is cheap and you don't need the method to mutate state. A pointer receiver method operates on the actual struct via a pointer, so modifications inside the method do affect the original - use this whenever the method needs to mutate the receiver's fields, or when the struct is large enough that copying it on every method call would be a meaningful performance cost. A common Go convention is to be consistent within a type - if any method needs a pointer receiver, use pointer receivers for all of that type's methods for consistency.
How does Go's garbage collector work, an: Go uses a concurrent, tri-color mark-and-sweep garbage collector designed to run mostly concurrently with your program to minimize stop-the-world pause times, rather than the longer full-stop pauses some other garbage-collected languages historically had. For performance-sensitive code, minimize unnecessary heap allocations (reusing buffers via `sync.Pool`, preferring value types over pointers where escape analysis would otherwise force heap allocation) since GC pressure scales with allocation rate - profiling with `pprof`'s memory profile reveals actual allocation hotspots rather than guessing, and Go's `GOGC` environment variable can tune the GC's aggressiveness/memory-tradeoff if genuinely needed after profiling confirms GC overhead is a real bottleneck.
What is a `sync.WaitGroup`, and how does: A `sync.WaitGroup` provides a simple counter-based mechanism - call `Add(n)` before launching n goroutines, each calls `Done()` when finished, and `Wait()` blocks until the counter reaches zero - purpose-built specifically for 'wait for a known set of goroutines to finish' with no data being passed back. Channels can achieve the same synchronization but are more naturally suited when you also need to pass data or results back from each goroutine (e.g. collecting each goroutine's result into a results channel) - WaitGroup is simpler and more idiomatic when you only need to know 'are they all done,' not collect anything from them.
How would you structure a Go module with: Organize by domain/responsibility rather than by technical layer - e.g. a top-level `cmd/` directory for entry points (main packages), an `internal/` directory for packages private to this module (preventing external modules from importing them, enforced by the Go toolchain), and packages within `internal/` organized around business domains (e.g. `internal/orders`, `internal/users`) rather than generic layers like `internal/models`, `internal/handlers` spread thin across every domain - this keeps related code (a domain's models, logic, and handlers) co-located and makes the module's structure reflect its actual business capabilities.
What is context.Context in Go used for,: `context.Context` carries cancellation signals, deadlines/timeouts, and request-scoped values across API boundaries and between goroutines - a parent context can be canceled (explicitly, or automatically when a deadline expires), and every goroutine holding a reference to it (or a derived child context) can check `ctx.Done()` to know it should stop work promptly. This is the standard Go pattern for propagating 'the caller gave up waiting, stop doing this work' through a chain of function calls and goroutines, preventing goroutine leaks where work continues indefinitely after nobody is waiting for the result anymore.
How would you profile a Go application f: Import `net/http/pprof` (for a running service, exposing profiling endpoints over HTTP) or use `go test -cpuprofile`/`-memprofile` for benchmarks, then analyze the resulting profile with `go tool pprof` - it shows exactly which functions consume the most CPU time or allocate the most memory, with a call graph showing where those calls originate from. This data-driven approach reveals the actual bottleneck (often surprising - not the function you'd have assumed) rather than guessing at optimization targets based on code that merely looks expensive.
What is a common pitfall with capturing: Before Go 1.22, a `for` loop's iteration variable was a single variable reused across all iterations, so launching goroutines inside the loop body that captured that variable by reference (`go func() { fmt.Println(i) }()`) would often all print the same final value of `i` once the loop finished, rather than each goroutine seeing the value it was launched with - a classic and surprising bug, fixed by explicitly creating a new local variable per iteration (`i := i`) before the goroutine or passing it as an argument. Go 1.22 changed the language semantics so each loop iteration gets its own fresh variable automatically, eliminating this entire class of bug going forward for code compiled against 1.22+.
How would you write table-driven tests i: Define a slice of test case structs (each with input values and expected output), then loop over them running the same test logic against each case with `t.Run(tc.name, func(t *testing.T) { ... })` for named subtests - this is idiomatic because it separates test data from test logic cleanly, makes adding a new test case as simple as adding one line to the slice rather than duplicating an entire test function, and `t.Run` subtests give clear per-case pass/fail reporting and let you run a single named case in isolation (`go test -run TestName/case_name`) when debugging a specific failure.
